Cyber Attack Disrupts Hong Kong Steel Industry Operations

A significant cyber attack targeting firms in Hong Kong’s steel industry has brought production and logistics to a standstill, with major players such as HBIS Group Hong Kong Co Ltd among those affected. The attack, which began on Wednesday morning, is believed to involve ransomware that has compromised IT infrastructure across several companies.

According to industry sources, steel processing plants and distribution networks are facing operational paralysis as computer systems controlling production lines, inventories, and shipping schedules have been encrypted by the attackers. HBIS Group Hong Kong Co Ltd confirmed in a statement Thursday that its internal systems had been "severely disrupted," resulting in the suspension of all order processing and outbound deliveries.

“The attack has forced us to halt all digital operations, and our teams are currently working with cybersecurity specialists to assess the extent of the breach,” said Eric Leung, head of operations at HBIS Group Hong Kong Co Ltd. “We recognise the impact on our customers and partners, and we are doing all we can to restore services.”

Industry analysts estimate that at least five mid-to-large steel firms in the city have been affected, with initial losses potentially exceeding HK$40 million if downtime extends through the week. Hong Kong’s Steel Manufacturers Association (HSMA) issued a statement urging members to remain vigilant and coordinate with authorities. “We are deeply concerned by the scale of disruption,” said HSMA spokesperson Connie Wong. “This incident highlights the vulnerability of industrial control systems and the urgent need for stronger cyber defences.”

The timing of the attack, just ahead of several major infrastructure project milestones in the region, has heightened concerns about supply delays and cost overruns. Local construction contractors have begun seeking clarification on delivery schedules for steel products.

Labour representatives have also voiced worries over job security if the outage continues. “Our members are facing uncertainty, with overtime shifts suspended and plant access restricted,” said Thomas Choi, secretary of the Hong Kong Metalworkers Union.

As of Thursday afternoon, the attack remains ongoing, with affected companies unable to access key data or resume normal operations. Law enforcement and cybersecurity agencies are investigating the incident, but no timeline has been given for full restoration of services. The steel industry is bracing for further disruptions if the situation is not resolved swiftly.
